Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42m
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Notes: discovery focused on private/VPC deployment, data residency, and private endpoint architecture. AE + SE from Redwood; CTO + Infra + Security from Bluegate.
summary: Bluegate is evaluating Redwood Private behind their VPC for PII-sensitive features. Key concerns: data residency to keep tokens in eu-west-1, private endpoints vs peering, egress IPs for allowlisting, KMS integration, SOC2 evidence. They asked about transit gateway vs peering recommendations and how Redwood handles fallback to Hosted/Dedicated if private capacity is constrained. Agreement to run a 4-week pilot and exchange network diagrams and a short checklist.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the account, and with me is Samira, our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Jordan (Bluegate - CTO): Yep, thanks. Jordan here. Really curious about how Redwood can run inside our VPC and satisfy EU residency requirements.
[00:14] Samira (Redwood SE): Great question. High level — Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC or connected via private endpoints. We support region pinning so you can keep inference traffic and logs in eu-west-1.
[00:24] Priya (Infra): When you say private endpoints, do you mean AWS interface endpoints, or some kind of sidecar inside our subnet? I'm trying to map to our network diagrams.
[00:33] Samira: Mostly interface endpoints / VPCEs in our middleware design, yes. Alternatively we can put a customer-hosted connector in your subnet that talks to the Redwood dataplane — both approaches have tradeoffs for maintenance and routing.
[00:44] Daniel (Security): And on encryption — KMS integration? We need to ensure keys are customer-managed and logs are accessible for audits.
[00:49] Samira: Absolutely. We integrate with customer KMS for model keys and can forward audit logs to your CloudWatch or Splunk. There are options for HSM backing if required.
[00:58] Jordan: Okay, good. Another thing — residency. Our legal team requires that data not leave EU borders. How airtight is region pinning?
[01:06] Alex: Region pinning means we deploy the inference capacity in the target region and make sure requests are routed there. For full assurance during pilot we can do a demonstration and provide traceroutes and egress IP ranges.
[01:16] Priya: Egress IPs are critical — we have an allowlist for external services. Will you provide a fixed set of IPs? Dynamic ranges aren't gonna fly.
[01:25] Samira: For Private deployments we can provide stable NAT egress IPs or provision customer-controlled NAT. If you use our private connector inside your VPC, egress is inside your control.
[01:33] Priya: So if we host the connector, all outbound to models stays inside our network? I'm concerned about calls to Redwood control plane for billing/rollouts.
[01:41] Samira: Right — control plane traffic is separate. In our Private architecture, the control plane can be either Redwood-managed (over an HTTPS control channel) or you can run a private control plane option — that latter is common for regulated customers. For the pilot we can start with a hybrid where the control plane talks over a tightly-scoped endpoint.
[01:56] Jordan: That hybrid makes sense for an initial run. What about peering vs transit gateway? Our infra team prefers transit gateway for scale but they're worried about cross-account routing.
[02:06] Samira: If you already have Transit Gateway, we typically recommend using it for many accounts to centralize routing — particularly if multiple VPCs need access. Peering is simpler for single-VPC setups. For low-latency critical paths, peering avoids an extra hop, but TGW gives more flexible policies.
[02:19] Priya: Hmm, latency — what's typical for inference inside an EU region? We aim for less than 120ms p95 for small-ish prompts.
[02:27] Alex: For an on-region Private deployment with minimal network hops we generally see sub-80ms p95 for 512-token-ish workloads on recommended instance types. But it'll depend on your subnet placement and NAT design.
[02:38] Jordan: Good, that aligns with our goals. Daniel, are there any compliance blockers on your end?
[02:42] Daniel: Main asks: SOC2 evidence, IAM roles and least privilege, key management, and auditability of prompts when they include PII. Also retention policies — can Redwood purge logs on demand?
[02:52] Samira: Retention is configurable per customer and per dataset; for Private deployments we can set retention to match your policy and provide deletion workflows. For SOC2 we have our report; for Private we can produce architecture diagrams and controls mapping.
[03:06] Priya: Can you talk about private endpoints in the context of cross-region requests? Suppose a user in eu-west-1 hits an endpoint but the model is in us-east-1 — do you do automatic fallback? That could violate residency.
[03:18] Samira: We route by policy. If you enable strict region pinning we disable cross-region fallback. We can also configure fallbacks to a smaller local model if needed. The key is establishing routing rules up front.
[03:31] Jordan: I want an explicit guarantee for the pilot: no cross-region model fallback unless we allow it.
[03:36] Alex: Noted — we'll add that to pilot constraints.
[03:38] Priya: Also curious about IP addressing — we run 10.0.0.0/16 across our main VPCs. Any recommendations for connector subnets?
[03:46] Samira: Keep connector subnets in separate /24s to simplify route tables and security groups. Avoid overlap with Redwood-managed CIDRs if using peering. We'll send a checklist with suggested CIDR ranges.
[03:56] Priya: Please do. Also, we need to know which ports/protocols to allow — is it just HTTPS 443?
[04:01] Samira: Mostly 443 for control and data planes. For metrics/tracing we might ask to open outbound to specific monitoring endpoints, but the default is 443.
[04:09] Jordan: On the subject of monitoring — can we get per-route latency and token usage forwarded into our observability stack?
[04:15] Alex: Yes, Redwood Console has token-level metrics, but in Private we can forward metrics via Prometheus exporters or push to your monitoring endpoint.
[04:24] Daniel: We also need to capture audit logs for prompt content — is that stored in your system or in our S3?
[04:30] Samira: For Private customers we can either keep logs local to your environment or stream logs to your S3 with server-side encryption using your KMS. We can mask or redact prompts prior to transfer if that's a requirement.
[04:44] Priya: Masking might be needed. We'll define examples of PII in the checklist.
[04:49] Jordan: What's the recommended path for short-term pilot vs long-term production? Say we do a 4-week pilot — what changes when we flip to prod?
[04:58] Samira: Pilot: a small dedicated pool or connector with restricted capacity, focused region pinning, and a handful of routes. Production: scale up to either Dedicated capacity reserved or full Private with autoscaling, and finalize network policies and SLA.
[05:13] Priya: If we need to scale quickly, how do you handle bursts? Do you move workloads to Hosted temporarily?
[05:18] Alex: We have policy-driven fallbacks. For strict residency customers we avoid cross-region Hosted fallbacks. We can do capacity bursting within your region via Dedicated on the same accounts if contracted. We'll propose options in the pricing playbook.
[05:30] Jordan: Pricing — we need a clear cost model for Private. E.g., what are the fixed infra costs vs variable tokens?
[05:37] Alex: We'll include line items: baseline infra (reserved capacity / connector overhead), per-request compute costs, storage/retention costs, and optional add-ons (extended retention, enhanced SLA, private control plane). We'll send a draft estimate for the pilot.
[05:51] Priya: Sweet. A few technical questions from my notebook — cross-account peering: if we bring a connector into a shared services VPC that peers to our app VPCs, do you support route propagation with TGW?
[06:03] Samira: Yes, TGW route propagation works fine with our connector. You'll just need to ensure route tables and security groups allow traffic to the connector subnets. We usually recommend a single shared services VPC hosting connectors for multi-account architectures.
[06:16] Daniel: For egress allowlisting, are there static HTTPS endpoints or IP ranges we should expect to whitelist?
[06:23] Samira: For managed Private we provide a set of egress IPs; if you're hosting the connector you'll control egress. We'll give you the list for the pilot.
[06:30] Jordan: Any limits on model sizes or quantization we should consider for on-prem connector mode?
[06:36] Samira: The connector handles requests and KV cache, but large models are hosted on Redwood's inference fleet. If you want fully local model hosting (self-hosted), that's a different engagement. For our Private offering we can serve common open models with optimized kernels; we'll recommend quantized variants for cost.
[06:50] Priya: So hybrid: control plane / orchestration from Redwood, compute either in our region on Redwood's fleet or fully customer-run if we go that route later.
[06:59] Samira: Exactly. Most customers start with Redwood-managed compute in-region and evolve to more customer-managed setups if needed.
[07:06] Jordan: Are there any compliance packages or contractual clauses for EU govt clients?
[07:11] Alex: We have data processing addenda and standard contractual clauses; for high compliance customers we can discuss dedicated control plane and custom language. We'll loop legal in later.
[07:20] Daniel: One more — we use Okta SAML for SSO. How does users/roles map into Redwood Private RBAC?
[07:27] Samira: We support SAML/SSO and can map Okta groups to Redwood roles. For Private we can also integrate with your IdP via SCIM for provisioning.
[07:35] Priya: Great. From a network operations perspective I need a clear playbook for outages — if Redwood region has a failure, what's the RTO assumed and how do we fail over safely without crossing borders?
[07:46] Alex: RTO depends on contract tier. For strict regional residency we avoid cross-region failover; instead we would route to a standby capacity within your region (Dedicated pool or customer-managed nodes). We'll outline options and RTO estimates in the pilot deck.
[07:58] Jordan: Let's discuss pilot success criteria now — what would Redwood recommend we measure?
[08:03] Samira: I'd propose: 1) latency p95 under agreed threshold (e.g., <120ms), 2) correctness/quality for a defined prompt set (we'll run evals), 3) network posture validated (private endpoints, allowlist ok), 4) security/retention controls verified.
[08:18] Priya: That sounds good. We can provide sample prompts and a baseline eval.
[08:23] Alex: Perfect. We'll prepare the pilot scope doc and share by 2026-04-09.
[08:28] Daniel: A small nit — how do you handle secret rotation for API tokens if we host connectors?
[08:33] Samira: We support short-lived tokens and automatic rotation. If using your KMS, you can rotate keys and we'll re-encrypt accordingly.
[08:40] Jordan: Any concern about route table scale if we have many connectors?
[08:44] Samira: Keep connectors in consolidated subnets and use TGW to reduce individual peering route entries. We can share an architecture note.
[08:52] Priya: Ok. For the legal procurement path — we need a high-level SOW and an estimate to start procurement. Can you give a timeline?
[08:59] Alex: After pilot acceptance, procurement typically takes 4-8 weeks depending on custom terms. We'll provide a pilot SOW and a pro forma contract for budget review.
[09:10] Jordan: Good. Any blockers from Redwood's side for a start date of April 20th?
[09:15] Samira: No blockers. We'll confirm resource availability and send a kickoff invite once the checklist items are exchanged.
[09:21] Priya: One last technical — do you support VPC endpoint policies to restrict who can call the endpoint?
[09:26] Samira: Yes, you can apply endpoint policies and SGs to limit callers. We'll include recommended policies in the checklist.
[09:33] Alex: Alright, quick recap: Redwood to send network checklist, pilot SOW, region egress IPs (if using managed connector), and a draft pricing estimate. Bluegate to share network diagrams, CIDR blocks, and compliance examples. Pilot targeted week of April 20th.
[09:50] Jordan: Sounds like a plan. Thanks, folks.
[09:52] Daniel: Thanks. We'll look out for the docs.
[09:54] Samira: Thanks everyone — will follow up with checklist.
[09:57] Alex: Talk soon.
[10:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional filler and overlaps; some product names transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "control plane" sometimes heard as "control planee").
